---
title: Fermenting sauerkraut
lang: en
free: true
---
Sauerkraut is made by lacto-fermentation of shredded cabbage: salt draws out cellular moisture, creating an anaerobic brine in which lactic acid bacteria (LAB) convert sugars into lactic and acetic acids. No starter culture is added; the bacteria—mainly _Leuconostoc mesenteroides_ in the early phase and _Lactobacillus plantarum_ later—are already present on the cabbage leaves.

## Salting and packing

Cabbage is shredded thinly and massaged with 2–2.5 % salt by weight—roughly one teaspoon per 500 g. Within minutes the salt draws liquid out of the leaves through osmosis, forming a natural brine. The cabbage is packed tightly into a clean jar, pressing down firmly so the brine rises above the shreds. Keeping the cabbage submerged below the brine surface is critical: any exposed pieces are vulnerable to mould and must be removed.

## Anaerobic fermentation

At room temperature (18–22 °C) fermentation is active within 24 hours, visible as small bubbles rising through the brine. The jar is left loosely covered to allow gas to escape while preventing oxygen from entering. After three to seven days a mild, pleasantly sour kraut is ready. Longer fermentation—two to four weeks in a cool cellar—develops deeper acidity and a more complex flavour, with the brine turning progressively more tangy and slightly effervescent.
